text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
Tasmanian pioneer GILBERT ROBERTSON, who was the editor of the first daily newspaper "True Colonist", was born in 1794. He spent so much time in jail for libel that the newspaper went broke.
Sydney solicitor BRENT RODD, whose Five Dock property is known as RODD Point, was born in 1809.
Australian cricketer FRED BOYLE, created the close-in fielding position "silly-mid-on", was born in 1847.
Pioneer Australian woman doctor JESSIE ASPINALL FREEMAN, who was the first female junior Resident Medical Officer at the Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney, was born in 1880.
American actress, DOROTHY LAMOUR, who was best-known for the "Road" films she made with BOB HOPE and BING CROSBY, was born in 1914.

British guitarist, singer and songwriter PETER SARSTEDT was born in 1942. He began his career by playing guitar in the backing band for his older brother RICHARD, who was successful under the name EDEN KANE. In the late sixties PETER started a solo career and had hits with "Where Do You Go To My Lovely?" and "Frozen Orange Juice" both in 1969. Attempts at further hits failed as did the group 'The SARSTEDT Brothers' with siblings RICHARD and CLIVE.
US guitarist with 'Kool and the Gang' BRENDEN HARKIN was born in 1948.

US country guitarist and singer JOHNNY RODRIGUEZ was born in 1951. He played with highschool rock bands and in 1971 went to Nashville and was with TOM T. HALL's band for two years. He was a successful solo artist on the country charts.
** EVENTS **
1901 : The first Nobel prizes were awarded to commemorate

the death of ALFRED NOBEL. He was a Swedish chemist and engineer who invented dynamite and other high explosives. These inventions made him extremely wealthy. He had died on the 10th December 1896 and his Will stated that five prizes be awarded annually for the most significant achievements in the fields of physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and services to the cause of peace.
1915 : The Ford Motor company made its one millionth

motor car. Six months later Ford announced a cut price 250 dollar touring car which was to be sold by garage operators rather than retail car outlets. The move was expected to increase Ford's already dominant share of the US car market.
1927 : Dog racing began at London's Wembley Stadium.
1938 : It was a day of serious bushfires in New South
Wales. It became known as Black Saturday.
1948 : The United Nations adopted a declaration of human
rights.
1949 : ROBERT MENZIES returned to power after a fear

campaign from the right linking Labor policy with Russian communism. MENZIES had declared socialism to be the key issue and it was BEN CHIFLEY's Bank Nationalisation Act which gave the opposition the ammunition it needed.
1963 : A state of emergency was declared in the South
Arabian Federation after a grenade was thrown at a group of government ministers and British diplomats at Aden airport.
1979 : Calcutta's Mother TERESA was awarded the Nobel

Peace Prize for her work with the destitute. She joined a convent at the age of 19 and in 1946 she was granted permission to leave the Calcutta convent and work in the community. In 1950 she formed the Missionaries of Charity. They now run more than 700 shelters and clinics. Mother TERESA has been described as a "living saint".
1983 : Democracy was restored in Argentina. Senor RAUL
ALFONSIN was inaugurated as the first civilian president for eight years.
1990 : Australia's oldest newspaper empire, the Fairfax
group, went into the hands of the receivers with debts of 1222 million dollars.
1991 : Government figures released in Britain revealed

the popularity of marriage was at an all-time low. The marriage rate in England was less than half that in 1971. Nearly one in three couples in their twenties were living together. At least one in ten marriages ended in divorce within five years and the divorce rate was growing at record speed. The rate of births outside marriage was also climbing and had almost tripled in ten years. More than 200,000 babies were born to unmarried parents in England and Wales in 1990.
